meta.title: Deep Time Atlas
meta.canonicalNote: All times are internally normalised to years before 2000 CE. Positive is past. The present is a negative number, which is deliberate: it keeps the origin fixed so the file does not silently change meaning next year.
meta.dataStatusNote: Values in this file are rough figures written from memory to prove the schema. Every record carries a src array that is currently either empty or points at the source that SHOULD supply it. Nothing here has been checked.

geo.note: The only lane here with an international standards body behind it.

records.label: Holocene
records.note: One of very few boundaries here fixed by ratified definition rather than estimate: a specific horizon in the NGRIP ice core.

records.label: Anthropocene?
records.note: Proposed as a formal epoch and voted down in 2024. Kept on the chart because the argument is real: proposed start dates have ranged from the Neolithic to the 1960s.

climate.note: Three separate records, each on its own scale. They measure different things, so they are not joined into one curve. A strip appears when the view shows enough of its time span.

strips.label: Deep-sea δ¹⁸O
strips.caption: Deep-sea δ¹⁸O · CENOGRID · up = warmer or less ice · not a temperature
strips.note: Oxygen isotopes in the shells of deep-sea foraminifera, from Westerhold et al. 2020 (CENOGRID). The value mixes deep-ocean temperature with the amount of ice on land, so it is not a temperature. Higher δ¹⁸O means colder or more ice, so the scale is flipped and up means warmer. The line is the source's own LOESS smoothing of its binned record (data/reference/benthic_d18o_cenogrid.csv).

strips.label: Antarctic temperature
strips.caption: Antarctic temperature · EPICA Dome C · °C vs the last 1,000 years · local, not global
strips.note: Temperature at Dome C, Antarctica, estimated from deuterium in the ice (Jouzel et al. 2007, EDC3 age scale), as a difference from the average of the last 1,000 years. It is a local record: polar swings are roughly twice the size of global ones (data/reference/antarctic_temperature_epica.csv).

strips.label: Global temperature
strips.caption: Global temperature · PAGES 2k · °C vs 1961–1990 · band: 95% range · dark line: instruments
strips.note: Global mean surface temperature reconstructed from proxies by the PAGES 2k Consortium (2019): the median of a 7,000-member ensemble with its 2.5–97.5% range, both as smoothed by the source over 31 years (16–1985 CE). The thin dark line is the instrumental record the reconstruction was checked against (Cowtan & Way, yearly, 1850–2017). Values are differences from 1961–1990 (data/reference/global_temperature_pages2k.csv).

hominins.note: Dates are the Smithsonian Human Origins Program's first and last appearances in a sparse fossil record. Absence of fossils is not absence of the species. Labelled bars are five well-established species, an editorial choice; the faint bars are the others.

records.label: S. tchadensis
records.name: Sahelanthropus tchadensis
records.note: Smithsonian: “Sometime between 7 and 6 million years ago”. One badly distorted skull. Whether it is a hominin at all is argued. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: O. tugenensis
records.name: Orrorin tugenensis
records.note: Smithsonian: “Sometime between 6.2 and 5.8 million years ago”. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: Ar. kadabba
records.name: Ardipithecus kadabba
records.note: Smithsonian: “Between about 5.8 and 5.2 million years ago”. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: Ar. ramidus
records.name: Ardipithecus ramidus
records.note: Smithsonian: “About 4.4 million years ago” (a single date, not a span). The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: Au. anamensis
records.name: Australopithecus anamensis
records.note: Smithsonian: “About 4.2 to 3.8 million years ago”. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: Au. afarensis
records.name: Australopithecus afarensis
records.note: Smithsonian: “Between about 3.85 and 2.95 million years ago”. Lucy's species; among the better-sampled early hominins. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: K. platyops
records.name: Kenyanthropus platyops
records.note: Smithsonian: “About 3.5 million years ago” (a single date, not a span). The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: Au. africanus
records.name: Australopithecus africanus
records.note: Smithsonian: “About 3.3 to 2.1 million years ago”. South African cave deposits are notoriously hard to date. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: P. aethiopicus
records.name: Paranthropus aethiopicus
records.note: Smithsonian: “About 2.7 to 2.3 million years ago”. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: Au. garhi
records.name: Australopithecus garhi
records.note: Smithsonian: “About 2.5 million years ago” (a single date, not a span). The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: H. habilis
records.name: Homo habilis
records.note: Smithsonian: “2.4 million to 1.4 million years ago”. Arguably a wastebasket taxon; some material may belong elsewhere. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: P. boisei
records.name: Paranthropus boisei
records.note: Smithsonian: “About 2.3 to 1.2 million years ago”. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: Au. sediba
records.name: Australopithecus sediba
records.note: Smithsonian: “Between 1.977 and 1.98 million years ago”. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: H. rudolfensis
records.name: Homo rudolfensis
records.note: Smithsonian: “About 1.9 million to 1.8 million years ago”. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: H. erectus
records.name: Homo erectus
records.note: Smithsonian: “Between about 1.89 million and 110,000 years ago”. The longest-lived member of our genus by a wide margin. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: P. robustus
records.name: Paranthropus robustus
records.note: Smithsonian: “About 1.8 to 1.2 million years ago”. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: H. heidelbergensis
records.name: Homo heidelbergensis
records.note: Smithsonian: “About 700,000 to 200,000 years ago”. Increasingly treated as a label of convenience rather than a species. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: H. neanderthalensis
records.name: Homo neanderthalensis
records.note: Smithsonian: “About 400,000 - 40,000 years ago”. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: H. naledi
records.name: Homo naledi
records.note: Smithsonian: “335,000 - 236,000 years ago”. The deposit's interpretation remains actively disputed. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: H. sapiens
records.name: Homo sapiens
records.note: Smithsonian: “About 300,000 years ago to present”. The boundary of 'anatomically modern' is a definition, not an observation. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

records.label: Denisovans
records.note: Defined largely from DNA plus a handful of fragments. The range is close to a guess.

records.label: H. floresiensis
records.name: Homo floresiensis
records.note: Smithsonian: “About 100,000 – 50,000 years ago”. Its dates have been revised drastically before. Expect more revision. The ends fade because the species probably lived before and after its first and last known fossils; how far the fade reaches is not from any source.

population.note: From 10,000 BCE to 2023 the line is Our World in Data's long-run world population series (data/reference/world_population_owid.csv). OWID joins three sources: HYDE 3.3 up to 1790, Gapminder v7 for 1800–1949 and UN World Population Prospects 2024 from 1950, and warns of possible breaks where they meet. It gives one central figure per year and no range. Figures before 1800 are model reconstructions, so that part of the line is dashed. Between 300,000 years ago and 10,000 BCE the shaded range is still an unsourced placeholder.

energy.note: Follows the general shape of Ian Morris's energy-capture index. The numbers are invented. This is the lane that makes the fossil-fuel discontinuity visible as something other than a date.

regions.note: Regional labels are conveniences of description, not entities that existed. They are also anachronistic before roughly 50 ka and misleading before 2 Ma, which is why this lane does not exist at those scales.

records.label: Neolithic
records.note: Where the fullest early evidence for farming survives — which is not the same as where it first happened.

records.label: Rome
records.note: The end date is a choice, not a fact. 476, 1453, or never, depending on what you think Rome was.

records.label: First settlement
records.note: One of the most actively disputed questions in archaeology. Claims run from about 15 ka to well over 30 ka, and the evidence at each end is contested on methodological grounds.

schemes.note: The point of this lane is disagreement. Switching schemes cuts the same millennia in incompatible ways, and one of them refuses to apply at all.

threeage.label: Three-age system
threeage.note: Devised by Christian Jürgensen Thomsen in 1830s Denmark to sort a museum collection. It was never meant as a universal history and does not work as one.

items.label: Bronze Age
items.note: Begins roughly 900 years later than in Anatolia. Same label, different world, and the label hides that.

items.label: Scheme does not apply
items.note: There is no Bronze Age here, and describing 65,000 years of continuous occupation as 'Stone Age' says more about the classifier than the classified. A periodisation built for Eurasia silently erases everywhere it does not fit.

bighistory.label: Big History thresholds
bighistory.note: David Christian's eight thresholds of rising complexity. Ambitious in scope, and openly teleological — it is a story with a direction built in.

items.label: 5 · Life
items.note: Loosely constrained and keeps moving earlier.

modes.label: Modes of production
modes.note: The Marxian sequence. Its universality was contested from the start, including by Marx, who worried openly about whether it applied outside Western Europe.

climate.label: Climate-led
climate.note: Periodisation by climate state rather than by material culture or politics. Rearranges what counts as a turning point.

items.label: Holocene stability
items.note: The unusually stable interval in which all agriculture, and therefore everything downstream of it, happened.

evidence.note: This lane is not about the past. It is about us: how much we can actually say, era by era. Currently hand-asserted step values. It should be computed — dated archaeological sites per millennium from p3k14c is the obvious candidate, which would make it an observation rather than an opinion.

co2.note: Atmospheric CO₂ in parts per million, on a log scale. Dots are individual proxy estimates from the CenCO2PIP Consortium (2023) data product, with their published uncertainty as faint bars: filled dots are the project's category 1 (high quality, uncertainty fully worked out), hollow dots category 2 (high quality, uncertainty not yet fully constrained). Category 3 (outdated methods) and estimates the project marks as superseded or quarantined are not shown. The line is the Antarctic ice-core composite (Bereiter et al. 2015); the dark line is Mauna Loa (NOAA and Scripps). Proxy CO₂ values are rounded to 0.1 ppm for the page; proxy ages, given in ka, are read as thousands of years before 2000, an offset of 50 years that cannot show at this scale.

ice.label: Antarctic ice cores
records: Dome C (Siegenthaler 2005 or Bereiter 2014; gap in source description)
EDML or Dome C sublimation (source ranges overlap)
ice.note: CO₂ measured in air bubbles trapped in Antarctic ice, from the composite of Bereiter et al. 2015 (data/reference/co2_ice_cores_bereiter.csv).

mlo.label: Mauna Loa
mlo.note: Annual mean CO₂ measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, by NOAA and Scripps since 1959 (data/reference/co2_mauna_loa_noaa.csv). Shown to 2023, the page's 'now'.

largestPolity.note: For every year from 3400 BCE to 2024, the polity with the largest mapped area in Cliopatria v0.2.1 (Seshat Global History Databank), computed from its map file (data/reference/largest_polity_by_year_cliopatria.csv). Area is the area of the drawn borders, not population. Cliopatria says its borders, names and dates are one version among disputed ones, and its coverage is thin in early periods: the count of polities it maps in a year is shown on hover. Names in brackets, such as '(British Empire)', are Cliopatria's composites of an empire and its member territories. Years are as Cliopatria gives them, negative for BCE.

highlights.label: The Holocene
highlights.note: A formally defined epoch, and one of the few boundaries on this chart with a ratified date attached to a physical layer in an ice core.

highlights.label: Agricultural revolution
highlights.note: Not an event and not one place: at least seven independent centres over several thousand years. The word 'revolution' is doing a great deal of work.

highlights.label: Fossil fuel era
highlights.note: Coal use is far older; sustained fossil-powered growth is roughly 250 years old. At full zoom-out on the linear axis this is thinner than the line drawn to represent it.

highlights.label: Out of Africa
highlights.note: The main dispersal. Earlier excursions are attested but seem to have left little genetic trace. Dates keep moving.

highlights.label: Last Glacial Maximum
highlights.note: Ice at maximum, sea level roughly 120 m lower. The coastlines people actually lived on are now underwater, which biases everything we think we know about this period.

highlights.label: Toba eruption
highlights.note: The eruption is firmly dated. Its supposed bottleneck effect on human populations is disputed and increasingly doubted.

highlights.label: Writing
highlights.note: The sharpest single change in evidence quality anywhere on this chart, and the reason the bottom strip steps up here.
